tests.label: Length order with alphabetical ties

comparator.hint: Compare length first and natural String order second.

requirements: Create a comparator with a length rule and an alphabetical tie-breaker.
Read the input values, calculate the answer, and print only the requested result.
input: Read n, the number of words.
Read the next n nonempty lowercase English words.
details.output: Print the sorted words, one word per line. If n is 0, print nothing.
constraints: Words contain only lowercase English letters.

examples.explanation: fig has 3 letters. kiwi and pear each have 4 letters, so kiwi comes before pear alphabetically.
There are no words to print.
One word is already sorted.

checks: Try the sample inputs first.
Check the boundary cases in the Test cases panel.

comparator.title: Absolute magnitude ordering
comparator.task: Sort integers by increasing absolute magnitude, then by increasing signed value. Convert to long before taking an absolute value so the smallest int is handled correctly.
comparator.hint: Compare the primary field first, returning to the next tie-breaker only when the primary comparison is zero.

requirements: Define a Comparator using safe comparisons and the stated tie-breakers; use it for ordering.
input: Read n then n signed 32-bit integers.
details.output: Print sorted values separated by spaces, or EMPTY.

examples.explanation: The (value, magnitude) pairs are []. Compare magnitudes first and signed values second; the magnitude of -2147483648 is 2147483648, which needs long.
The (value, magnitude) pairs are [(-2147483648, 2147483648)]. Compare magnitudes first and signed values second; the magnitude of -2147483648 is 2147483648, which needs long.
The (value, magnitude) pairs are [(4, 4), (-4, 4), (1, 1), (-1, 1), (0, 0)]. Compare magnitudes first and signed values second; the magnitude of -2147483648 is 2147483648, which needs long.

comparator.title: Even values before odd values
comparator.task: Sort all even integers before all odd integers. Inside each parity group, use increasing numeric order.
comparator.hint: Compare the primary field first, returning to the next tie-breaker only when the primary comparison is zero.

requirements: Define a Comparator using safe comparisons and the stated tie-breakers; use it for ordering.
input: First n, then n integers in their original order; any remaining tokens are described below. All indexes are zero-based.
details.output: Print the sorted values, or EMPTY.
constraints: 0<=n<=500; each value is between -1000000 and 1000000. Use long for sums.

examples.explanation: The even values in increasing order are []; the odd values are []. Concatenate the even group and then the odd group.
The even values in increasing order are [0]; the odd values are []. Concatenate the even group and then the odd group.
The even values in increasing order are [-2, 0, 4, 4]; the odd values are [1]. Concatenate the even group and then the odd group.

comparator.title: Distance from a pivot
comparator.task: Sort numbers by increasing absolute distance from a given pivot. Break equal-distance ties by increasing numeric value.
comparator.hint: Compare the primary field first, returning to the next tie-breaker only when the primary comparison is zero.

requirements: Define a Comparator using safe comparisons and the stated tie-breakers; use it for ordering.
input: First n, then n integers in their original order; any remaining tokens are described below. All indexes are zero-based. After values read pivot, -1000000<=pivot<=1000000; calculate differences in long.
details.output: Print sorted values, or EMPTY.
constraints: 0<=n<=500; each value is between -1000000 and 1000000. Use long for sums.

examples.explanation: For pivot 0, the (value, distance) pairs are []. Smaller distance wins, with smaller signed value resolving an equal distance.
For pivot 4, the (value, distance) pairs are [(0, 4)]. Smaller distance wins, with smaller signed value resolving an equal distance.
For pivot 1, the (value, distance) pairs are [(4, 3), (1, 0), (4, 3), (-2, 3), (0, 1)]. Smaller distance wins, with smaller signed value resolving an equal distance.

comparator.title: Binary digit-count order
comparator.task: Sort numbers by the number of one bits in the binary representation of their absolute magnitude. Break ties by increasing signed value; zero has zero one bits.
comparator.hint: Compare the primary field first, returning to the next tie-breaker only when the primary comparison is zero.

requirements: Define a Comparator using safe comparisons and the stated tie-breakers; use it for ordering.
input: First n, then n integers in their original order; any remaining tokens are described below. All indexes are zero-based.
details.output: Print sorted values, or EMPTY.
constraints: 0<=n<=500; each value is between -1000000 and 1000000. Use long for sums.

examples.explanation: The records (value, binary magnitude, one-bit count) are []. Order by the final count, then signed value; zero contributes no one bits.
The records (value, binary magnitude, one-bit count) are [(0, '0', 0)]. Order by the final count, then signed value; zero contributes no one bits.

The records (value, binary magnitude, one-bit count) are [(4, '100', 1), (1, '1', 1), (4, '100', 1), (-2, '10', 1), (0, '0', 0)]. Order by the final count, then signed value; zero contributes no one bits.

comparator.title: Case-insensitive word order
comparator.task: Order ASCII words by lowercase spelling. When lowercase spellings tie, order by the original case-sensitive spelling.
comparator.hint: Compare the primary field first, returning to the next tie-breaker only when the primary comparison is zero.

requirements: Define a Comparator using safe comparisons and the stated tie-breakers; use it for ordering.
input: Read n then n words.
details.output: Print sorted words one per line, or EMPTY.
constraints: 0<=n<=500; words are 1..20 ASCII letters; uppercase letters precede lowercase letters in case-sensitive order.

examples.explanation: The comparison keys (lowercase, original) are []. Compare the first strings and then the original strings, so capitalization breaks a lowercase tie.
The comparison keys (lowercase, original) are [('a', 'a')]. Compare the first strings and then the original strings, so capitalization breaks a lowercase tie.

The comparison keys (lowercase, original) are [('tea', 'tea'), ('eat', 'eat'), ('dog', 'dog'), ('ate', 'ate'), ('god', 'god')]. Compare the first strings and then the original strings, so capitalization breaks a lowercase tie.

comparator.title: Nulls last
comparator.task: Treat the token NULL as a null String and every other token as a word. Sort non-null words lexicographically and put all null entries last.
comparator.hint: Compare the primary field first, returning to the next tie-breaker only when the primary comparison is zero.

requirements: Use Comparator.nullsLast around the non-null String comparator.
input: Read n then n tokens; NULL denotes null and is not an ordinary word.
details.output: Print ordered tokens on one line separated by spaces, displaying nulls as NULL; print EMPTY for n=0.
constraints: 0<=n<=500; non-null words contain 1..20 ASCII letters and are not NULL.

examples.explanation: The non-null words sort to []. The 0 NULL entries go after every word and remain separate entries.
The non-null words sort to []. The 1 NULL entries go after every word and remain separate entries.
The non-null words sort to ['a', 'b', 'b']. The 1 NULL entries go after every word and remain separate entries.

comparator.title: Reverse alphabetical words
comparator.task: Sort words in decreasing case-sensitive lexicographic order. Equal words remain separate output entries.
comparator.hint: Compare the primary field first, returning to the next tie-breaker only when the primary comparison is zero.

requirements: Define a Comparator using safe comparisons and the stated tie-breakers; use it for ordering.
input: Read n then n words.
details.output: Print words one per line in reverse lexical order, or EMPTY.

examples.explanation: The increasing case-sensitive order is []. Reading that order backward gives the requested decreasing order, retaining all duplicates.
The increasing case-sensitive order is ['a']. Reading that order backward gives the requested decreasing order, retaining all duplicates.

requirements: Use recursion to reduce the unprocessed part of the line.
input: One complete line of text; do not trim its spaces.
details.output: Print the reversed line; an empty input line produces an empty output line.
constraints: 0<=line length<=200; ASCII letters and spaces only.

examples.explanation: Character positions are [(0, 'l'), (1, 'e'), (2, 'v'), (3, 'e'), (4, 'l')]. Recursive unwinding emits positions [4, 3, 2, 1, 0], preserving each character including spaces.
The line has zero characters, so the recursive base case has no character to emit or mismatched pair to find.
Character positions are [(0, 'a')]. Recursive unwinding emits positions [0], preserving each character including spaces.

recursion.title: Recursive palindrome test
recursion.task: A palindrome reads identically from either end. Compare corresponding characters recursively; the empty string is a palindrome.
recursion.hint: Compare the outer characters, then recurse inward.

requirements: Use recursion to reduce the unprocessed part of the line.
input: One complete line of text; do not trim its spaces.
details.output: Print YES or NO, with comparisons case-sensitive.
constraints: 0<=line length<=200; ASCII letters and spaces only.

examples.explanation: Compare positions 0 and 4: 'l' and 'l'; Compare positions 1 and 3: 'e' and 'e'; Compare positions 2 and 2: 'v' and 'v'. The line is a palindrome exactly when every compared pair matches.
The line has zero characters, so the recursive base case has no character to emit or mismatched pair to find.
Compare positions 0 and 0: 'a' and 'a'. The line is a palindrome exactly when every compared pair matches.

recursion.title: Remove adjacent runs recursively
recursion.task: Keep only the first character of each maximal run of equal adjacent characters. Preserve character order and case.
recursion.hint: Compare each character with its immediate predecessor before retaining it.

requirements: Use recursion to reduce the unprocessed part of the line.
input: One complete line of text; do not trim its spaces.
details.output: Print the compressed string; print an empty line for an empty string.
constraints: 0<=line length<=200; ASCII letters and spaces only.

examples.explanation: The adjacent runs are ['l' repeated 1, 'e' repeated 1, 'v' repeated 1, 'e' repeated 1, 'l' repeated 1]. Retain one character from each run, including one space for a run of spaces.
The line has zero characters, so the recursive base case has no character to emit or mismatched pair to find.
The adjacent runs are ['a' repeated 1]. Retain one character from each run, including one space for a run of spaces.

recursion.title: Divide-and-conquer maximum
recursion.task: Split the array into smaller ranges and recursively find the largest value. Negative values are valid and must not be replaced by a default zero.
recursion.hint: Return a present value for a nonempty base case so all-negative ranges work.

requirements: Use recursion; inversion counting should combine sorted halves.
input: n followed by n integer values.
details.output: Print the maximum, or EMPTY for n=0.

examples.explanation: Split [4, 2, 7] into [4] and [2, 7]. Their maxima 4 and 7 are compared on return.
The range is empty: it has no maximum or matching position, and contributes no values, inversion pairs, or merge work.
Split [0] into [] and [0]. The single value 0 is already the base-case maximum.

recursion.title: Recursive array total
recursion.task: Compute the total of all array values by recursively combining subproblems. An empty array has total zero.
recursion.hint: Split into smaller ranges and combine their returned totals.

requirements: Use recursion; inversion counting should combine sorted halves.
input: n followed by n integer values.
details.output: Print the sum.

examples.explanation: The input contributes (4) + (2) + (7). Each position belongs to exactly one recursive base case, so no value is counted twice.
The range is empty: it has no maximum or matching position, and contributes no values, inversion pairs, or merge work.
The input contributes (0). Each position belongs to exactly one recursive base case, so no value is counted twice.

recursion.title: Merge-sort inversion count
recursion.task: An inversion is a pair of indexes i<j with value[i]>value[j]. Count all such pairs; equal values are not inversions.
recursion.hint: During merging, a smaller right value precedes every remaining left value.

requirements: Use recursion; inversion counting should combine sorted halves.
input: n followed by n integer values.
details.output: Print the inversion count.

examples.explanation: The qualifying (leftIndex,rightIndex,leftValue,rightValue) records are [(0, 1, 4, 2)]. Equal values and pairs in increasing value order are excluded.
The range is empty: it has no maximum or matching position, and contributes no values, inversion pairs, or merge work.
The qualifying (leftIndex,rightIndex,leftValue,rightValue) records are []. Equal values and pairs in increasing value order are excluded.

recursion.title: Merge work across recursion
recursion.task: Merge sort splits a range of length n into floor(n/2) left items and the rest right items. Every merge of a range with length at least two contributes that full range length to the work count.
recursion.hint: Add the current range length only when a split and merge actually occur.

requirements: Use recursion; inversion counting should combine sorted halves.
input: n followed by n integer values.
details.output: Print total merge work; lengths zero and one contribute zero.

examples.explanation: The ranges that actually merge have lengths [3, 2]. Summing those lengths counts each merge layer, while singleton leaves add zero.
The range is empty: it has no maximum or matching position, and contributes no values, inversion pairs, or merge work.
The ranges that actually merge have lengths []. Summing those lengths counts each merge layer, while singleton leaves add zero.

recursion.title: Recursive first-match search
recursion.task: Search a nondecreasing array for target. If target is repeated, report its first index.
recursion.hint: When a match is found, recursively search the left half for an earlier match.

requirements: Use recursive binary search with index bounds.
input: n followed by n sorted integer values, then target.
details.output: Print the smallest zero-based matching index, or -1.

examples.explanation: bounds [0,2] inspect index 1, value 4; bounds [0,0] inspect index 0, value 2. Continue left after a possible match to find the first 4; insertion position 1 matches.
The range is empty: it has no maximum or matching position, and contributes no values, inversion pairs, or merge work.
bounds [0,0] inspect index 0, value 0. Continue left after a possible match to find the first 0; insertion position 0 matches.

recursion.title: Memoized combination count
recursion.task: Count ways to choose k items from n distinct items, where order does not matter. Use C(n,k)=C(n-1,k-1)+C(n-1,k), with boundary counts one.
recursion.hint: Cache states by both n and k; boundary rows and diagonal entries are one.

requirements: Use recursive memoization over both n and k.
input: Two integers n k.
details.output: Print C(n,k).

examples.explanation: Split choices according to whether one distinguished item is selected: C(4,1)=4 and C(4,2)=6. These disjoint groups cover all choices.
k=0 is a boundary choice for n=0: selecting nothing has exactly one subset.
k=0 is a boundary choice for n=1: selecting nothing has exactly one subset.

recursion.title: Count Fibonacci call instances
recursion.task: Consider a recursive function that always counts its current invocation and, when n>=2, calls itself for n-1 and n-2. Count invocation instances of this naive recursion, including repeated states.
recursion.hint: Count the current invocation plus both child invocation totals, even for repeated states.

requirements: Compute the recursive call-count recurrence.
input: One integer n.
details.output: Print total function invocations, including the initial call.

examples.explanation: The current invocation contributes 1, its n=4 branch contributes 9, and its n=3 branch contributes 5. Repeated states in those branches still count as separate invocations.
At n=0, the function executes once and makes no child calls.
At n=1, the function executes once and makes no child calls.

backtracking.title: Index-mask subsets
backtracking.task: Generate every subset of the input positions, treating repeated values at different positions as distinct. A mask bit i is one when zero-based position i is selected. Explore choices with backtracking.

backtracking.title: Binary strings
backtracking.task: Generate every string of length n made only of 0 and 1. Keep leading zeros and place the strings in dictionary order, with 0 before 1.

requirements: Generate the choices using backtracking. Do not print spaces between the bits.
Read the input values, calculate the answer, and print only the requested result.

details.output: Print each different n-character string on its own line.

examples.explanation: The four length-2 strings are 00, 01, 10, and 11.

backtracking.title: Distinct value permutations
backtracking.task: Generate all different arrangements using every input occurrence exactly once. Duplicate occurrences must not create duplicate output lines. Explore choices with backtracking.
backtracking.hint: Sort values first and skip equal choices at the same recursion depth.

requirements: Use backtracking to explore choices and undo state.

details.output: Print arrangements in numeric lexicographic order, one per line; print EMPTY for the single empty arrangement.

Value multiplicities are []. Using every entry selects nothing, giving one empty arrangement rather than zero arrangements.
Value multiplicities are [(0, 1)]. There are 1 position permutations before equal-value copies are merged; ordered choices begin with [0].

backtracking.title: Unique sorted subsets
backtracking.task: Generate every distinct multiset subset. Within each subset sort values increasingly; choosing different occurrences that produce identical values counts only once. Explore choices with backtracking.

requirements: Use backtracking to explore choices and undo state.
input: n followed by n integer values.
details.output: Print distinct subsets in numeric lexicographic order (a shorter equal prefix comes first), one per line; write EMPTY for the empty subset.

examples.explanation: The 8 position masks reduce to 8 distinct sorted value sequences. For example, initial choices are [[], [1], [1, 3], [1, 3, 5]]; matching value sequences from different masks are kept once.

backtracking.title: Even-sized subset count
backtracking.task: Count position-based subsets containing an even number of entries. The empty subset is included, and duplicate values at different positions are distinct choices. Explore choices with backtracking.

backtracking.title: Permutations without neighboring equals

graphs.title: Strong component labels
graphs.task: Vertices are strongly connected when each can reach the other through directed edges. Number strongly connected components by increasing smallest vertex ID.
graphs.hint: Two vertices share a component when each reaches the other.

details.output: Print component labels in vertex-ID order, beginning at label 0.
constraints: 1<=n<=40; 0<=m<=n*(n-1); no loops or repeated directed edges; path counts fit long because a DAG has at most 40 vertices.

graphs.task: Count directed source-to-destination paths in a directed acyclic graph. If the input has any directed cycle, report that instead; the zero-edge path counts when source equals destination.

requirements: Use directed graph algorithms and respect edge direction.
input: n m followed by m directed edges u v, meaning u to v. Vertex IDs are 0..n-1.
After edges read source destination, both in 0..n-1.

Initialize source 2 with one zero-edge path and every other vertex with zero. No edges propagate counts; destination 2 retains its initial count.

graphs.task: Each undirected edge has a nonnegative travel cost. Find minimum total cost from source to each vertex; a zero-cost edge is valid.
graphs.hint: Use long distances and discard stale priority-queue entries.

input: n m followed by m lines u v weight for undirected edges, then source, also in 0..n-1.

constraints: 1<=n<=100; 0<=m<=1000; 0<=weight<=1000000000; no loops or repeated edges; use long totals.

dynamic-programming.title: Minimum unlimited coin count
dynamic-programming.task: Choose as few coins as possible to make the exact amount. Each positive denomination can be used any number of times; repeated denominations describe the same coin type.
dynamic-programming.hint: Let the state for an amount try every possible final coin.

requirements: Use dynamic programming over amounts.
input: n followed by n coin denominations, then amount.
details.output: Print the minimum number of coins, or -1 if impossible; amount=0 requires 0 coins.

examples.explanation: Two coins of value 3 make 6. No single available coin is worth 6, so two is the minimum.
Amount zero is already reached with no coins, even though no denominations are supplied.
Every sum of coins worth 2 is even. Amount 3 is odd, so it cannot be reached.

dynamic-programming.title: Climbing stairs
dynamic-programming.task: You are at the bottom of a staircase with n steps. On each move you may climb either 1 step or 2 steps. Count the different sequences of moves that land exactly on step n.
dynamic-programming.hint: Use long, base ways[0]=1, and combine ways from one and two steps earlier.

requirements: Read the input values, calculate the answer, and print only the requested result.
input: Read the number of steps n.
details.output: Print the number of ordered ways. For n = 0, print 1 for the one way of making no moves.
constraints: The answer fits in a Java long.
Order matters: 1 then 2 is a different sequence from 2 then 1.

examples.explanation: For 5 steps, the eight sequences are 11111, 1112, 1121, 1211, 2111, 122, 212, and 221.
Doing nothing is one valid way to climb zero steps.
The only way to climb one step is a single move of size 1.

dynamic-programming.title: Unordered coin combinations
dynamic-programming.task: Count combinations of coins that make the exact amount when each denomination may be reused. Changing coin order does not create a new combination, and repeated denominations count once.
dynamic-programming.hint: Process each distinct denomination once, then update amounts in increasing order.

requirements: Use a dynamic programming table with long counts.
input: n followed by n coin denominations, then amount.
details.output: Print the number of combinations; the empty combination counts once for amount=0.

examples.explanation: The four combinations are six 1s; three 1s and one 3; two 3s; and two 1s and one 4. Rearranging a combination does not count again.
Choosing no coins is the one combination that makes zero.
Coins worth 2 cannot make the odd amount 3, so there are zero combinations.

dynamic-programming.title: One-use knapsack value
dynamic-programming.task: Choose items with total weight at most capacity to maximize total value. Each listed item may be chosen at most once, even when two items have equal weight and value.
dynamic-programming.hint: The capacity update direction determines whether the current item can be reused.

requirements: Use dynamic programming over capacity.
input: n capacity followed by n lines weight value.
details.output: Print maximum total value; choosing nothing is allowed.

examples.explanation: Choose the items of weights 2 and 3. Their total weight is 5 and their total value is 6 + 10 = 16, greater than the value 12 of the weight-4 item.
There are no items and capacity is zero. Choosing nothing has value zero.
The only item weighs 2, exceeding capacity 1. It cannot be selected.

dynamic-programming.title: Reusable knapsack value
dynamic-programming.task: Choose items with total weight at most capacity to maximize total value. Each listed item type may be used any number of times.
dynamic-programming.hint: The capacity update direction determines whether the current item can be reused.

requirements: Use dynamic programming over capacity.
input: n capacity followed by n lines weight value.
details.output: Print maximum total value; choosing nothing is allowed.

examples.explanation: One weight-2 item and one weight-3 item fill capacity 5 with value 16. Repeating the weight-2 item gives only value 12; the weight-4 item also gives 12.
No item types are available, so no positive value can be collected.
Even one copy of the weight-2 item exceeds capacity 1. Reuse cannot help it fit.

dynamic-programming.title: Subset total reachability
dynamic-programming.task: Decide whether some subset of input positions has sum target. Each position can be selected at most once, and the empty subset is permitted.
dynamic-programming.hint: Update reachable totals downward so one input position cannot be reused.

requirements: Use dynamic programming over achievable sums.
input: n followed by n nonnegative integers, then target.
details.output: Print YES or NO.

examples.explanation: Choosing positions 0 and 1 gives 2 + 3 = 5, so the target is reachable.
The empty subset contains no positions and has sum zero, matching the target.
Both choosing the zero and choosing nothing make zero. Existence alone is enough to print YES.

dynamic-programming.title: Count position subsets
dynamic-programming.task: Count subsets of input positions whose values add to target. Equal values at different positions are different choices, including separate zero values.
dynamic-programming.hint: Initialize one way to make zero and let each position contribute choose-or-skip counts.

requirements: Use dynamic programming with long counts.
input: n followed by n nonnegative integers, then target.
details.output: Print the subset count, including the empty subset when target=0.

examples.explanation: Only the subset of positions 0 and 1 makes 5: 2 + 3 = 5. The value 7 cannot be part of such a subset.
There is one subset of an empty input: the empty subset. Its sum is zero.
There are two position subsets: skip the zero or select it. Both have sum zero, so count both.

dynamic-programming.title: Closest two-group totals
dynamic-programming.task: Assign every value to one of two groups, either of which may be empty. Minimize the absolute difference between the two group sums.

dynamic-programming.title: Strictly increasing subsequence
dynamic-programming.task: Choose a subsequence by deleting zero or more entries without reordering those that remain. Find the greatest length whose values are strictly increasing, so equal neighbors cannot both extend it.

requirements: Use dynamic programming on the two word prefixes.

dynamic-programming.title: Longest palindromic subsequence
dynamic-programming.task: Choose characters in their original order so that the selected sequence reads the same forward and backward. Find the maximum possible length, allowing deletions between chosen characters.
dynamic-programming.hint: Use interval states and compare the two end characters.

requirements: Use interval dynamic programming.
input: One complete line containing a lowercase word, possibly empty.

dynamic-programming.title: Grid routes around blocks
dynamic-programming.task: Travel from upper-left to lower-right using only right and down moves through open cells. Count all routes; a blocked start or destination prevents every route.

dynamic-programming.title: Minimum right-down path sum
dynamic-programming.task: Move from upper-left to lower-right using only right and down. Minimize the sum of all visited cell values, counting both endpoints.

dynamic-programming.hint: Use the cheapest of the three valid predecessor columns.

requirements: Use dynamic programming one row at a time.
input: rows cols followed by rows lines of cols integer values.
